insight.insight: Standard SAE features already show temporal persistence that varies by feature. After a feature activates, the hidden state stays aligned with its decoder direction, and past activations help reconstruct later states, but only in globally coherent documents. Making this explicit with a diagonal EMA state per feature, with a learned decay coefficient λ_j trained by reconstruction alone, lets the model discover a spectrum of feature timescales without predefined temporal partitions. Fast (low-λ) features stay locally interpretable, while slow (high-λ) features carry context.
dependent_results: Section 3 / Appendix D: median empirical persistence for BatchTopK on Pythia falls from 0.618 (lag 1) to 0.160 (lag 64) and is 0.096 at lag 512. The shuffled control decays to about 0. Power-law exponents are β_nat≈0.32 vs β_shf≈0.87–0.92.

Section 3 / D.1: lag-1 context correction removes 0.89% (Pythia BatchTopK) and about 0.40% (Gemma) of reconstruction error, while shuffled controls stay slightly below zero. 76–91% of lag-1 weights are positive (mean about 0.07–0.09), against a shuffled mean of about 0.

Section 5.1 / Table 1: Persistent SAE stays competitive on reconstruction. FVE is 0.93 vs 0.94 for BatchTopK on Pythia, and 0.66 vs 0.72 on Gemma. Slow features are much smoother (0.05 Pythia, 0.04 Gemma) than baselines (≥0.12).
Section 5.1 / Figure 3: quintiles with higher λ_j have higher median empirical persistence R_j(τ) across lags, whereas the Temporal SAE's predefined groups are not clearly separated.
Section 5.2 / Table 1: fast features get autointerp scores of 0.93 (Pythia) and 0.89 (Gemma), matching or exceeding the best baselines. Slow features score lower (0.84, 0.79).
Section 5.2 / Figure 4: lowest-λ features are updated more often at nouns, and highest-λ features more often at punctuation and conjunctions.

Section 5.3 / Figures 5–6: in t-SNE, slow features form clearer MMLU subject clusters than baselines or raw hidden states. For subject probing, selecting features by decreasing λ nearly matches the supervised oracle, and the slowest 1% reach high AUC.

Section 5.4 / Figure 7: on AgentDojo prompt injection, fast and standard SAE features detect injections best at d=0 but fall toward chance by 350 tokens, while the slow state retains signal. Slow-feature steering directions give the largest, consistently positive Δ_causal at every distance, whereas baseline directions give near-zero or negative effects.
key_definitions: Section 2: a standard SAE reconstructs x̂ = W_dec f + b_dec with sparse non-negative f. Feature j has normalised decoder direction d_j and is active when f_j > 0.

Section 3: the projection p_j^(t) = d_j^T x^(t). Empirical persistence R_j(τ) is the elevation of p_j at lag τ after activation, relative to the elevation at the activating token, both measured against the mean projection. R=1 means fully retained; R=0 means back to baseline.
Section 3: the shuffled control concatenates intact sentences from different Pile documents, preserving local but not global continuity.
Section 3: context correction x̂_ctx = x̂_base + W_dec(w_τ ⊙ f^(t−τ)). R²_improve is the fraction of baseline reconstruction error this recovers on held-out data.

Section 4: Persistent SAE state h_j^(t) = λ_j h_j^(t−1) + (1−λ_j) a_j^(t), where a is the BatchTopK token-wise sparse activation. Reconstruction is x̂ = W_dec h + b_dec. h^(0) = 0 at the start of each sequence.
Section 4 / B.3: λ_j = λ_max σ(l_j), with λ_max = 0.999 and logits initialised to 0.5. The recurrence is an EMA, so the state magnitude stays bounded.
Section 5.1: slow features are the top 1% by λ_j, and fast features are the bottom 50%.
Section 5.2: relative update frequency U_{q,c} = P(token category c | active feature in quintile q) / P(c).
Section 5.4: Δ_causal is half the difference in the monitor's yes−no logit margin when adding vs subtracting a probe-weighted decoder direction v_r scaled to 10% of the hidden-state norm.
reasoning_steps: Section 3: if standard SAE features retain decoder-aligned signal after activation more strongly in natural than in shuffled documents, the persistence reflects document-level context rather than local coherence.

Section 3: if past activations along the same feature direction reduce held-out reconstruction error only with the true history, then standard SAEs leave usable temporal structure unexploited. Because persistence varies across features, a per-feature timescale is warranted.

Section 4: a diagonal per-feature recurrence with learnable λ_j lets reconstruction gradients raise λ_j when carrying a feature forward helps later reconstructions and lower it otherwise. Timescales are thus learned without partitions or auxiliary temporal losses, and the diagonal form keeps attribution to decoder directions.

Section 5.1: competitive FVE and cosine similarity show the persistent state does not sacrifice reconstruction. The λ distribution and the λ-quintile ordering of R_j(τ) validate that the learned coefficients reflect real timescales.

Section 5.2: evaluating the token-wise activation a shows fast features remain locally interpretable. Slow features describe broad domains and are updated at punctuation and conjunctions, which motivates evaluating them jointly as a context state.

Section 5.3: if the slow state encodes context, it should cluster by subject and support subject probing. Ranking by λ then serves as an unsupervised feature-selection criterion that approaches a label-based oracle.

Section 5.4: a probe trained at the end of the injected span and tested later measures signal retention. Steering with probe-weighted decoder directions tests whether that signal is causally used by the monitor, showing slow states carry the signal over long contexts while fast features handle local detection.
